name: Dandelion extract
lead: Dandelion extract is a preparation from the leaves, roots or flowers of Taraxacum officinale, the common dandelion, a perennial of the daisy family (Asteraceae) native to Eurasia [1]. The leaves, flowers and roots are used as food and in herbal medicine, and extracts are sold as teas, capsules and tinctures [1].

In appearance communities dandelion is used for one reason: its long reputation as a diuretic. People who want a leaner, less puffy face and a sharper physique look for ways to shed temporarily retained water, and herbal diuretics such as dandelion are discussed for that purpose, as well as in physique-sport circles and in liver-support lists among anabolic steroid users [15][16][17]. The plant is traditionally linked to urination: its French folk name pissenlit and English folk name piss-a-bed refer to it, and leaves have been used as a diuretic in Chinese medicine for roughly 2,000 years [1]. The diuretic effect is attributed to the plant's high potassium content [1]. A 2009 human study of a leaf extract over one day reported promising diuretic results while the authors called for further research [1].

No published trial has tested dandelion extract for facial puffiness. Most laboratory research concerns antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer and animal-nutrition effects in cells and animals rather than humans [3][4][6]. Memorial Sloan Kettering's patient resource describes human evidence as limited, with the single-day diuretic study among the few human data points [18].

paras: Taraxacum officinale is a perennial herb growing from a generally unbranched taproot, with milky latex and a rosette of basal leaves 5 to 45 cm long. Leafless stems carry single yellow flower heads of 40 to over 100 florets, and many lineages set seed without fertilisation (apomixis). It is native to Europe and Asia and has been introduced to the Americas, southern Africa, Australasia and India [1].

Potassium is a major component of the leaves and is the usual explanation offered for the diuretic effect [1]. Raw greens are rich in vitamin K, with vitamin A, vitamin C, iron and calcium also listed [1]. The root contains inulin-type polysaccharides, and its latex holds a serine proteinase called taraxalisin [1]. Sesquiterpene lactones are considered the allergens [18].

Young leaves and buds are eaten in salads and older leaves cooked; flowers are used in dandelion wine, and roasted roots make a caffeine-free coffee substitute [1]. Supplements come as teas, capsules, tinctures and extracts, and dandelion is also an ingredient in multi-herb bloating and digestive products [9].

Linnaeus described the species in 1753 as Leontodon taraxacum [1]. The genus name probably derives from an Arabic term meaning bitter herb, and the physician Al-Razi used the word for dandelions, chicory and endive; Gerard of Cremona spelled it tarasacon around 1170 [1]. The English name comes from the French dent de lion, lion's tooth, for the toothed leaves [1]. The species has been used in European, North American and Chinese traditional medicine for diuresis, digestion and liver complaints [1][18].

Traditional uses include diuresis, digestion, liver and gallbladder complaints, appetite stimulation and, in Chinese medicine, Taraxacum mongolicum for breast abscess and mastitis [1][5][18]. In appearance contexts, dandelion root or leaf is mentioned in forum discussions as an herbal diuretic for water retention and bloating, as well as in liver-support stacks used by people on anabolic steroids [15][16][17].

The diuretic effect is traditionally attributed to potassium [1]. Laboratory work reports antioxidant activity and inhibition of inflammatory signalling in cell and animal models, including macrophage and zebrafish studies and oxidative-stress models in bovine mammary cells [3][6][11]. In rats, dandelion extract reduced oxidative stress in carbon tetrachloride liver injury through CYP2E1 suppression [12]. Cell studies of Taraxacum mongolicum in breast cancer lines report effects on cell stress and signalling [5]. Memorial Sloan Kettering notes that animal and laboratory data suggest lipid-lowering, liver-protective, anti-inflammatory and diuretic effects, and that estrogenic activity and increased proliferation of hormone-sensitive breast cancer cells have also been reported in preclinical work [18].

Dandelion belongs to the Asteraceae (Compositae) family, and contact allergy to Compositae plants is a recognised clinical entity studied with patch testing and described in people with atopic dermatitis [13][14]. Memorial Sloan Kettering lists heartburn, stomach upset, mild diarrhea at high intake, rash or contact dermatitis, allergic reactions and reported low blood sugar as adverse effects, along with case reports of hemorrhagic cystitis with a slimming product containing dandelion, acute liver injury with a herbal detox tea, and raised immunosuppressant levels in a kidney transplant recipient [18].

The same source describes possible additive effects with diuretics and diabetes medicines, and laboratory evidence that dandelion inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 enzymes and may affect UGT enzymes, which could alter drug levels [18]. Herbal products vary in quality and composition.
No studies found on dandelion extract for facial puffiness or depuffing.

Related research: the 2009 single-day study reported promising diuretic effects of dandelion leaf and called for further work [1]. Memorial Sloan Kettering also cites a randomized trial of a multi-herb product containing dandelion for tonsillitis in children, which does not isolate dandelion [18]. Registered human trials include a trial of dandelion in obese perimenopausal women (n=120) [7], a small trial of dandelion juice in hand eczema (n=4) [8], and bloating-supplement trials in which dandelion may be one of several ingredients [9]. Other published work consists of in vitro, animal and veterinary studies, such as antioxidant effects in cells, dairy cows and fish, and in vitro gallstone dissolution [4][6][10].

lore.intro: On T Nation, dandelion root is occasionally mentioned as an herbal diuretic for water retention and as a component of liver-support supplement lists.[15][16]

claims.claim: Dandelion root or leaf works as an herbal diuretic that reduces water weight and bloating.
claims.believers: A forum member advised that dandelion root, an herbal diuretic, could help a person whose weight fluctuated through water retention.[15]
claims.experts: The traditional diuretic reputation is long-standing, and one 2009 study reported promising results, but further studies were called for; no trial has tested it for facial puffiness.[1]

claims.believers: Users discussing steroid use suggest dandelion root extract, tea and similar herbs for liver and kidney support.[16][17]
claims.experts: Laboratory research reports antioxidant effects in rat liver injury and cell models, but no human trial of liver protection has been reported.[12][6]

chain: Leaf or root extract taken as a mild herbal diuretic
Less retained water, a leaner-looking face and midsection
angle.text: People use dandelion tea or capsules hoping for temporary water loss that makes the face look less puffy and the physique look more defined. The diuretic reputation is traditional and one small human study found promising results; its effect on facial appearance has not been measured.
